result:
The first time I darned a sock, I sewed it to the knee of my trousers. This is an easy mistake to make if you are concentrating on being the sort of person who darns socks rather than on the needle emerging underneath one.

I sat still for a minute. The sock was blue, the trousers brown. Together they suggested a poor map of a coastal inlet. I could reach the scissors if I leaned far enough, but every time I leaned, the inlet narrowed and my knee came up.

Eventually my daughter walked through the kitchen. “Did you mean to do that?” she asked.

“No.”

She handed me the scissors. I appreciated the absence of a second question.

Once detached, the sock was quite serviceable. The patch made a little ridge beneath my heel, which I noticed all the way to the post office and forgot about on the way home. I wore it for another winter. When its partner disappeared, I slipped the survivor over a jar of screws so the glass wouldn't knock against the other jars in my toolbox.

Yesterday my daughter called to ask how to mend a cuff. I told her to put a rolled towel inside the sleeve, gave her my best account of the stitch, and waited while she tried it. Through the phone I could hear rain on her windowsill, a bus changing gears outside, then the small hard tap of her scissors closing.

“How is it?” I asked.

“Go on,” she said.
